Where it began

Shahid Afridi was born on 1 March in Tirah, in the Khyber region of north-west Pakistan, one of a large family of brothers and sisters. He grew up on tales of Pakistan's 1992 World Cup win, and later said that tournament shaped his cricket and taught him not to fear failure.

He came through the under-19 circuit in the mid-1990s, and in one season for Karachi Whites he took 42 wickets in five matches at 9.59 apiece.

The player

He announced himself in October 1996. He did not bat on his one-day debut against Kenya, but in his next game, against Sri Lanka, he went in at number three and reached a hundred from 37 balls, then the fastest in one-day internationals, with eleven sixes along the way.

His Test debut came against Australia in October 1998, by which time he had already played 66 one-day games. Opening the batting, he took five wickets in the first innings, and in his second Test, in India the following January, he made 141. In 27 Tests between 1998 and 2010 he scored 1,716 runs at 36.51, with five hundreds and a best of 156, and took 48 wickets.

His finest hour came in the shorter game. At the 2007 Twenty20 World Cup he became the first man to be named player of that tournament, and two years later he made 54 not out and took 1 for 20 in the final as Pakistan won it. He went on to captain his country, and at the 2011 World Cup he shared the lead for wickets with 21.

What made him special

Nobody needed to ask what he was going to do. Ravi Shastri named him Boom Boom after a 26-ball fifty against India in 2005, and when bowlers were polled that year on the batters they most feared in one-day cricket, only Adam Gilchrist and Brian Lara came out ahead of him. Wasim Akram reckoned he changed how openers approached Test batting.

Caution was not part of the package, so the big scores came in bursts rather than every week. He himself said he thought of himself as a bowler first, and his brisk leg-breaks, googly and quicker ball brought him a great many wickets. Rashid Khan grew up idolising him and copying his action.

Away from the middle

In 2014 he set up the Shahid Afridi Foundation to bring schooling and healthcare to people in Pakistan, and he joined UNICEF's campaign against polio. A 2015 list of the most generous athletes in the world included him. He also served briefly as Pakistan's interim chief selector. Pakistan honoured him with the Pride of Performance and the Sitara-i-Imtiaz.

And finally

He had to wait until his 256th Twenty20 match, for Hampshire in 2017, to make a hundred in the format. For a man who once needed only 37 balls in a one-day game, that may be the most patient thing he ever did.
